text: Chest discomfort: Chest pain is pain or discomfort in the chest, typically the front of the chest. It may be described as sharp, dull, pressure, heaviness or squeezing.
Edema: Edema or oedema, also known as dropsy, hydropsy, fluid retention, or simply swelling, is the buildup of fluid in a bodily tissue. Most commonly, the legs or arms are affected.

Exertional dyspnea: Shortness of breath (SOB), known as dyspnea or dyspnoea, is an uncomfortable feeling of not being able to breathe well enough. The American Thoracic Society defines it as "a subjective experience of breathing discomfort that consists of qualitatively distinct sensations that vary in intensity", and recommends evaluating dyspnea by assessing the intensity of its distinct sensations, the degree of distress and discomfort involved, and its burden or impact on the patient's activities of daily living.

Orthopnea: Orthopnea or orthopnoea is shortness of breath (dyspnea) that occurs when lying flat, causing the person to have to sleep propped up in bed or sitting in a chair. It is commonly seen as a late manifestation of heart failure, resulting from fluid redistribution into the central circulation, causing an increase in pulmonary capillary pressure and causing difficulty in breathing.
Palpitations: Palpitations occur when a person becomes aware of their heartbeat. The heartbeat may feel hard, fast, or uneven in their chest.
Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea: PND may refer to:.

Presyncope: Lightheadedness is a common and typically unpleasant sensation of dizziness or a feeling that one may faint. The sensation of lightheadedness can be short-lived, prolonged, or, rarely, recurring.

Syncope: Syncope or Syncopy may refer to:Syncope (medicine), also known as fainting or passing out, a loss of consciousness
Syncope (phonology), the loss of one or more sounds, particularly an unstressed vowel, from the interior of a word
Syncopation, a musical effect caused by off-beat or otherwise unexpected rhythms
Syncopation (dance), or syncopated step, a step on an unstressed beat
Suspension, in music
Syncope (frog), a genus of microhylidae frogs
Syncopy Inc., a British film production company.
Unilateral leg swelling: A presenting complaint characterised by unilateral leg swelling.

Acute Coronary Syndrome: Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is a syndrome due to decreased blood flow in the coronary arteries such that part of the heart muscle is unable to function properly or dies. The most common symptom is centrally located pressure-like chest pain, often radiating to the left shoulder or angle of the jaw, and associated with nausea and sweating. Common presenting complaints: Chest Discomfort, Exertional Dyspnea, Presyncope, Syncope, Palpitations. Associated symptoms: Chest Discomfort, Sweating, Nausea, Radiation Arm Jaw. Risk factors: Hypertension, Smoking, Diabetes, Dyslipidemia, Family History CAD. Age relevance: adult. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: acute.
Acute Coronary Syndrome red flags. Red flag (RED_CARD_006) triggered by complaint 'EXERTIONAL_DYSPNEA': New severe chest discomfort with dyspnea — emergency pathway.

Acute Coronary Syndrome differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Stable Ischemic Heart Disease: SIHD chest discomfort is exertional and predictable; ACS is new worsening or occurs at rest. Compared to Pericarditis: Pericarditis pain is positional/pleuritic; ACS pain is typically pressure-like and exertion-related.

Aortic Stenosis: Aortic stenosis is the narrowing of the outlet of the main pumping chamber of the heart, the left ventricle (LV). If the narrowing is severe the extra work required from the left ventricle to pump the blood against the increased resistance of a small orifice may cause thickening of the heart muscle, followed by severe weakness of the heart. Common presenting complaints: Exertional Dyspnea, Presyncope, Syncope. Associated symptoms: Chest Discomfort, Fatigue. Risk factors: Older Age, Congenital Bicuspid Valve, Calcific Degeneration. Age relevance: elderly_predominant. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: chronic.
Aortic Stenosis red flags. Red flag (RED_CARD_002) triggered by complaint 'SYNCOPE': Syncope during exertion — classic AS red flag, urgent evaluation.
Aortic Stenosis differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Mitral Regurgitation: AS murmur is systolic ejection radiates to carotids; MR is holosystolic radiates to axilla.

Atrial Fibrillation: Atrial fibrillation is an abnormal heart rhythm (arrhythmia) characterized by rapid and irregular beating of the atrial chambers of the heart. It often begins as short periods of abnormal beating, which become longer or continuous over time. Common presenting complaints: Palpitations, Presyncope, Syncope, Exertional Dyspnea. Associated symptoms: Fatigue, Dizziness, Exercise Intolerance. Risk factors: Hypertension, Older Age, Valvular Disease, Alcohol Use, Sleep Apnea. Age relevance: elderly_predominant. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: both.
Atrial Fibrillation red flags. Red flag (RED_CARD_003) triggered by complaint 'PALPITATIONS': Palpitations with syncope — urgent evaluation.

Atrial Fibrillation differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Supraventricular Tachycardia: SVT is regular and typically abrupt onset/offset; AFib is irregularly irregular. Compared to Ventricular Tachycardia: VT is a wide-complex often hemodynamically unstable rhythm; AFib is narrow-complex and irregular.

Bradyarrhythmia: Bradycardia, also called bradyarrhythmia, is a resting heart rate under 60 beats per minute (BPM). While bradycardia can result from various pathological processes, it is commonly a physiological response to cardiovascular conditioning or due to asymptomatic type 1 atrioventricular block. Common presenting complaints: Presyncope, Syncope, Exertional Dyspnea. Associated symptoms: Fatigue, Dizziness, Exercise Intolerance. Risk factors: Older Age, Conduction System Disease, Medication Induced. Age relevance: elderly_predominant. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: chronic.
Bradyarrhythmia red flags. Red flag (RED_CARD_002) triggered by complaint 'SYNCOPE': Syncope during exertion — urgent cardiovascular evaluation.
Bradyarrhythmia differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Ventricular Tachycardia: Bradyarrhythmia has abnormally slow rate; VT has abnormally fast rate - opposite ends of the rhythm spectrum.

Cardiomyopathy: Cardiomyopathy is a group of primary diseases of the heart muscle. Early on there may be few or no symptoms. Common presenting complaints: Exertional Dyspnea, Orthopnea, PND, Palpitations, Syncope, Edema. Associated symptoms: Fatigue, Exercise Intolerance. Risk factors: Family History Cardiomyopathy, Alcohol Use, Previous Viral Myocarditis. Age relevance: all. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: chronic.
Cardiomyopathy red flags. Red flag (RED_CARD_002) triggered by complaint 'SYNCOPE': Syncope during exertion — urgent cardiovascular evaluation.
Cardiomyopathy differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Myocarditis: Myocarditis has recent viral illness and acute onset; cardiomyopathy is typically more gradual or has a family/toxin history.

Heart Failure: Heart failure (HF), also known as congestive heart failure (CHF), is a syndrome caused by an impairment in the heart's ability to fill with and pump blood. Common presenting complaints: Exertional Dyspnea, Orthopnea, PND, Edema, Palpitations, Presyncope, Syncope, Unilateral Leg Swelling. Associated symptoms: Fatigue, Exercise Intolerance, Weight Gain, Cough. Risk factors: Hypertension, Coronary Artery Disease, Diabetes, Previous MI. Age relevance: all. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: both.

Heart Failure red flags. Red flag (RED_CARD_005) triggered by complaint 'EXERTIONAL_DYSPNEA': Severe breathlessness at rest. Red flag (RED_CARD_002) triggered by complaint 'SYNCOPE': Syncope during exertion in known/suspected heart failure. Red flag (RED_CARD_004) triggered by complaint 'UNILATERAL_LEG_SWELLING': Sudden breathlessness plus unilateral leg swelling — route to PE/DVT pathway.

Heart Failure differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Pulmonary Hypertension: Criteria: ECHO EF (HF typically shows poor LVEF; PH shows isolated RV dilation with normal LV systolic/diastolic function). Symptoms: HF features prominent orthopnea and pulmonary crackles; PH has exertional dyspnea without orthopnea/PND. Compared to Hypertensive Heart Disease: HHD driven primarily by long-standing uncontrolled hypertension without another structural cause.

Hypertensive Heart Disease: Hypertensive heart disease is a chronic condition where long-standing high blood pressure leads to structural and functional changes in the heart, including left ventricular hypertrophy and eventual heart failure. Common presenting complaints: Exertional Dyspnea, Orthopnea, PND, Edema. Associated symptoms: Fatigue, Headache. Risk factors: Hypertension, Obesity, Older Age. Age relevance: adult. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: chronic.

Hypertensive Heart Disease differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Heart Failure: HHD is driven primarily by chronic hypertension; HF may have multiple structural causes and more pronounced congestive symptoms.

Mitral Regurgitation: Mitral regurgitation is a condition where the mitral valve fails to close properly, causing blood to flow backward from the left ventricle into the left atrium during systole. Common presenting complaints: Exertional Dyspnea, Orthopnea, PND, Edema. Associated symptoms: Fatigue, Palpitations. Risk factors: Previous MI, Mitral Valve Prolapse, Rheumatic Heart Disease. Age relevance: all. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: chronic.
Mitral Regurgitation differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Aortic Stenosis: MR murmur is holosystolic radiating to axilla; AS murmur is systolic ejection radiating to carotids.

Myocarditis: Myocarditis is inflammation of the cardiac muscle. Myocarditis can progress to inflammatory cardiomyopathy when there is associated ventricular remodeling and cardiac dysfunction due to chronic inflammation. Common presenting complaints: Exertional Dyspnea, Palpitations, Presyncope, Syncope. Associated symptoms: Chest Discomfort, Fatigue, Recent Viral Illness. Risk factors: Recent Viral Infection, Young Age, Autoimmune Disease. Age relevance: young_adult_predominant. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: acute.
Myocarditis red flags. Red flag (RED_CARD_002) triggered by complaint 'SYNCOPE': Syncope during exertion — urgent cardiovascular evaluation.
Myocarditis differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Pericarditis: Pericarditis pain is positional/pleuritic; myocarditis pain is less positional and paired with arrhythmia/heart-failure signs.

Pericarditis: Pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium, the fibrous sac surrounding the heart. Symptoms typically include sudden onset of sharp chest pain, which may also be felt in the shoulders, neck, or back. Common presenting complaints: Exertional Dyspnea. Associated symptoms: Positional Chest Pain, Fever, Pleuritic Chest Pain. Risk factors: Recent Viral Infection, Autoimmune Disease, Recent MI Or Cardiac Surgery. Age relevance: all. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: acute.

Pericarditis differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Acute Coronary Syndrome: Pericarditis pain worsens lying flat and improves leaning forward; ACS pain is typically pressure-like unaffected by position.

Pulmonary Embolism: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a blockage of an artery in the lungs by a substance that has moved from elsewhere in the body through the bloodstream (embolism). Symptoms of a PE may include shortness of breath, chest pain particularly upon breathing in, and coughing up blood. Common presenting complaints: Exertional Dyspnea, Unilateral Leg Swelling, Presyncope, Syncope. Associated symptoms: Sudden Breathlessness, Pleuritic Chest Pain, Tachycardia. Risk factors: Immobilization, Recent Surgery, Malignancy, Pregnancy, Long Haul Travel. Age relevance: all. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: acute.

Pulmonary Embolism red flags. Red flag (RED_CARD_004) triggered by complaint 'UNILATERAL_LEG_SWELLING': Sudden breathlessness plus unilateral leg swelling — PE/DVT emergency pathway. Red flag (RED_CARD_001) triggered by complaint 'EXERTIONAL_DYSPNEA': Sudden severe breathlessness — emergency pathway.
Pulmonary Embolism differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Heart Failure: PE has sudden onset and usually unilateral leg swelling; HF has gradual onset and typically bilateral edema.

Pulmonary Hypertension: Pulmonary hypertension is a condition of increased blood pressure in the arteries of the lungs. Symptoms include shortness of breath, fainting, tiredness, chest pain, swelling of the legs, and a fast heartbeat. Common presenting complaints: Exertional Dyspnea, Presyncope, Syncope, Edema. Associated symptoms: Fatigue, Exercise Intolerance. Risk factors: Chronic Lung Disease, Left Heart Disease, Connective Tissue Disease, Chronic PE. Age relevance: all. Sex relevance: female_predominant. Acute or chronic: chronic.
Pulmonary Hypertension red flags. Red flag (RED_CARD_002) triggered by complaint 'SYNCOPE': Syncope during exertion — urgent cardiovascular evaluation.

Pulmonary Hypertension differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Heart Failure: Criteria: ECHO EF (PH shows isolated RV dilation with normal LV systolic/diastolic function; HF typically shows poor LVEF). Symptoms: PH has exertional dyspnea without orthopnea/PND; HF features prominent orthopnea and pulmonary crackles.

Stable Ischemic Heart Disease: Stable ischemic heart disease is a chronic condition characterized by reduced blood flow to the heart muscle due to atherosclerotic coronary artery disease, leading to exertional chest pain and other ischemic symptoms that are typically relieved by rest or nitroglycerin. Common presenting complaints: Chest Discomfort, Exertional Dyspnea. Associated symptoms: Chest Discomfort, Fatigue. Risk factors: Hypertension, Smoking, Diabetes, Sedentary Lifestyle, Older Age. Age relevance: adult. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: chronic.
Stable Ischemic Heart Disease differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Acute Coronary Syndrome: ACS presents with new worsening or rest symptoms; SIHD is stable and exertion-predictable.

Supraventricular Tachycardia: Supraventricular tachycardia is a rapid heart rhythm originating above the ventricles, often causing palpitations, dizziness, and shortness of breath. Common presenting complaints: Palpitations, Presyncope, Syncope. Associated symptoms: Sudden Rapid Heartbeat, Dizziness, Chest Discomfort. Risk factors: Congenital Heart Disease, Older Age. Age relevance: all. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: acute.
Supraventricular Tachycardia red flags. Red flag (RED_CARD_003) triggered by complaint 'PALPITATIONS': Palpitations with syncope — urgent evaluation.
Supraventricular Tachycardia differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Atrial Fibrillation: AFib is irregularly irregular; SVT is regular with abrupt onset/offset.

Ventricular Tachycardia: Ventricular tachycardia is a rapid heart rhythm originating from the ventricles that can lead to hemodynamic instability and sudden cardiac death. Common presenting complaints: Palpitations, Presyncope, Syncope. Associated symptoms: Dizziness, Chest Discomfort, Hemodynamic Instability. Risk factors: Previous MI, Coronary Artery Disease, Cardiomyopathy History. Age relevance: adult. Sex relevance: both. Acute or chronic: acute.

Ventricular Tachycardia red flags. Red flag (RED_CARD_003) triggered by complaint 'PALPITATIONS': Palpitations with syncope — treat as emergency until proven otherwise. Red flag (RED_CARD_002) triggered by complaint 'SYNCOPE': Syncope during exertion — urgent cardiovascular evaluation.
Ventricular Tachycardia differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Supraventricular Tachycardia: VT is wide-complex and frequently unstable; SVT is narrow-complex and usually stable.
Sudden severe breathlessness - action: emergency pathway.
Syncope during exertion - action: urgent cv evaluation.
Palpitations with syncope - action: urgent evaluation.
Sudden breathlessness + unilateral leg swelling - action: pe dvt red flag pathway.
Severe breathlessness at rest - action: emergency pathway.
New severe chest discomfort + dyspnea - action: emergency pathway.
